prompt: Each consumer has used a product and compared it with what they expected. Name the outcome the expectancy disconfirmation model predicts.

cases.text: From the booking photos, Lena expected an ordinary hotel room. She is given a room with a sea view and a free breakfast.
cases.explanation: Perceived performance exceeded her prepurchase expectations, producing high satisfaction or delight.

cases.text: Omar's new running shoes feel exactly as comfortable as the reviews said they would.
cases.explanation: Perceived performance matched his expectations, producing baseline satisfaction.

cases.text: An ad promised a blender that crushes ice in seconds. At home, it struggles with soft fruit.
cases.explanation: Perceived performance fell short of the expectations created by advertising, producing dissatisfaction.

cases.text: Mei bought a budget phone expecting a basic camera. Its photos turn out as sharp as her friend's far more expensive phone.
cases.explanation: Perceived performance exceeded what she expected from a budget phone.

cases.text: Ken orders his usual coffee at the cafe near work. It tastes the way it always does, which is what he expected.
cases.explanation: Perceived performance matched his expectations: simple confirmation.

cases.text: A streaming service advertised thousands of new films. After signing up, Ana finds only a handful she has not already seen.
cases.explanation: Advertising raised her prepurchase expectations, and perceived performance fell below them.

prompt: Match each attribution dimension or outcome with the question or case that illustrates it after a service failure.

pairs.match: A shopper asks whether a cracked phone screen was caused by their own drop or by weak factory glass.
pairs.explanation: Locus of causality asks whether responsibility lies internally with the consumer or externally with the firm or environment.

pairs.match: A traveler checks whether an airline delay came from a rare blizzard or from chronic understaffing.
pairs.explanation: Stability asks whether the cause is temporary and unusual or permanent and systemic.

pairs.match: A diner asks whether a restaurant could have prevented a food shortage by ordering ingredients on time.
pairs.explanation: Controllability asks whether the firm had the power to foresee and prevent the failure.

pairs.match: A subscriber learns that their internet outage resulted from the provider ignoring routine maintenance for months.
pairs.explanation: Anger and desire for retaliation peak when a failure is attributed to an external, stable, and firm-controllable cause.

question_text: Which of these purchases is most likely to leave the buyer with severe postpurchase cognitive dissonance?
hint: Think about the price, irrevocability, social or psychological involvement, and whether rejected alternatives had distinct attractive features.
correct_answer_citation: Week 9: Cognitive Dissonance and Buyer's Regret

options.option_text: A $2 bottle of water bought at a kiosk on a hot day
options.option_explanation: The purchase is inexpensive, low involvement, and trivial, so there is little cause for postpurchase dissonance.

options.option_text: A $1,800 sofa sold as final sale, chosen over two attractive competing models with washable covers that the chosen sofa lacks
options.option_explanation: Correct. It is expensive, irrevocable, and high involvement, and the rejected alternatives offered desirable features the chosen option lacks.

options.option_text: The pack of gum the shopper buys every week at the checkout
options.option_explanation: A low-cost habitual purchase gives the buyer little reason to experience postpurchase dissonance.

options.option_text: A $40 sweater that can be returned within 30 days for a full refund
options.option_explanation: The purchase is modest in price and easily reversible, which keeps postpurchase dissonance low.

prompt: Each card describes how a dissatisfied customer responds after a bad purchase. Sort the actions into Singh's (1988) three pathways.

cards.text: Maya brings a faulty toaster back to the store counter and asks the manager for a replacement.
cards.explanation: Voice responses direct the complaint toward the seller itself to seek redress.

cards.text: Devon emails the airline's customer-care team requesting a voucher after his luggage is delayed.
cards.explanation: Contacting the seller directly for compensation is a voice response.

cards.text: Priya stops visiting a dry cleaner that ruined her coat and warns three coworkers never to use it.
cards.explanation: Quietly exiting the relationship and warning acquaintances is a private response.

cards.text: Carlos says nothing to the cafe that served him burnt espresso and simply buys coffee across the street from then on.
cards.explanation: Silent brand switching without notifying the seller is a private exit response.

cards.text: Elena files a formal complaint with a government consumer-protection agency against a contractor.
cards.explanation: Escalating the dispute to an external regulatory institution is a third-party response.

cards.text: Tariq posts a detailed one-star warning on a public review platform so strangers will avoid the hotel.
cards.explanation: Publishing a complaint on an external public review platform is a third-party response.

prompt: What is each consumer doing with a product? Sort the cards into Jacoby, Berning, and Dietvorst's (1977) three primary disposition branches.

cards.text: Nadia continues riding her ten-year-old bicycle to work every day.
cards.explanation: She keeps the product and continues using it for its original function.

cards.text: Paul cuts his worn-out cotton T-shirts into cleaning rags for the garage.
cards.explanation: He keeps the product and converts it to a new secondary function.

cards.text: Ali packs the family camping tent into the attic closet until next summer.
cards.explanation: He keeps the product by storing it unused.

cards.text: Ruth lends her power drill to a neighbor for the weekend.
cards.explanation: Lending the item to a peer is a temporary disposition.

cards.text: Theo rents out his cinema lens for a week through a peer-to-peer gear sharing platform.
cards.explanation: Renting an item out through a sharing platform is a temporary disposition.

cards.text: Ines throws her broken umbrella into the municipal trash bin.
cards.explanation: Throwing an item away is a permanent disposition.

cards.text: Marco donates his son's outgrown winter coats to a neighborhood charity.
cards.explanation: Giving an item away is a permanent disposition.

cards.text: Yuki trades in her old game console at an electronics retailer for credit toward a new model.
cards.explanation: Trading an item in is a permanent disposition.

question_text: An online retailer offers a 10-dollar store credit in its postpurchase review solicitation email and wants to maximize the share of buyers who submit a review. Based on Wadi et al. (2026a, 2026b), which framing should the retailer pair with the reward?
hint: Compare how a generalized social-exchange appeal ('help other shoppers') and a direct reciprocal-exchange appeal ('help our company') perform when paired with a financial incentive.
correct_answer_citation: Week 9: Social Exchange Versus Reciprocal Exchange in Review Solicitation (Wadi et al., 2026a, 2026b)

options.option_text: Ask buyers to 'help our company improve,' because reciprocal exchange maximizes the number of people who submit a review
options.option_explanation: Reciprocal exchange with the company caused the minority who responded to write longer reviews, but lowered overall participation.

options.option_text: Avoid mentioning other shoppers, because financial rewards crowd out social-exchange norms completely
options.option_explanation: In the studies, pairing the financial reward with 'help other shoppers' outperformed pairing the same reward with 'help the company.'

options.option_text: Ask buyers to 'help other shoppers make informed decisions,' pairing the financial reward with a social-exchange appeal
options.option_explanation: Correct. Asking buyers to help other shoppers produced higher review submission rates than asking them to help the company, both alone and when paired with a 10-dollar credit.

options.option_text: Use either phrasing interchangeably, because solicitation framing has no effect once a 10-dollar credit is offered
options.option_explanation: Even with the same 10-dollar credit, the shopper-focused appeal significantly outperformed the company-focused appeal.

prompt: Each consumer has a distinct combination of relative attitude and repeat patronage. Identify the loyalty condition from Dick and Basu's (1994) matrix.

cases.text: Dana buys the same dish soap every month only because it sits at eye level in her nearest convenience store. She holds no preference for it over other brands.
cases.explanation: High repeat patronage combined with a weak relative attitude, driven by shelf habit and convenience.

cases.text: Luis admires an artisanal espresso machine brand and praises its engineering, but its high price prevents him from buying it.
cases.explanation: A strong favorable attitude combined with low repeat purchase due to price or distribution barriers.

cases.text: Grace flies the same airline consistently, prefers its service over rivals, and refuses competitor promotional discounts.
cases.explanation: A strong, favorable relative attitude combined with high repeat patronage.

cases.text: Noah sees all alkaline battery brands as interchangeable and grabs whichever multi-pack is on display at the hardware counter.
cases.explanation: Weak relative attitude combined with low repeat patronage toward any single brand.

prompt: Each card shows an instruction a consumer gives an AI shopping agent for routine replenishment. Sort the instructions into brand-directed delegation or agent-reliant delegation.

cards.text: "Reorder the same 15-pound bag of Blue Ridge dog food I bought last month."
cards.explanation: The consumer holds attitudinal loyalty and explicitly names the brand in the prompt.

cards.text: "Buy unscented clumping cat litter at the lowest price per pound."
cards.explanation: The consumer states only a category goal and delegates brand selection to the agent.

cards.text: "Get me two more boxes of my usual 12-ounce Brand X green tea."
cards.explanation: Explicitly specifying the usual brand constrains the agent to repurchase that brand.

cards.text: "Order dishwasher tablets with the best value and at least a 4.5-star rating."
cards.explanation: Under agent-reliant delegation, the agent evaluates available listings from scratch based on the stated goal and storefront attributes.

cards.text: "Replenish paper towels. Pick whichever listing gives the most sheets per dollar."
cards.explanation: Prior purchase habit does not constrain the agent when only an optimization goal is given.

cards.text: "Order the exact sulfate-free shampoo brand from my saved favorites list."
cards.explanation: Naming the preferred brand in the instruction protects the brand during automated replenishment.
